records.quote: However, we found that by the time a branch resolves and its misprediction is revealed, many in-flight instructions have already finished execution, thereby enlarging the set of values visible to the predictor when it restarts, and this fact can be exploited.
records.why: The paper confirms that instructions finishing execution before misprediction resolution enlarge the available values visible upon restart.

records.claim: The writeback completion handler updates the register status digest table with the computed digest and sets the valid bit when an instruction writing a destination register completes.
records.quote: When the instruction completes, we overwrite the payload with the digest of the produced value and set the valid bit.
records.why: The paper explicitly states that instruction completion triggers overwriting the entry's payload with the digest and asserting valid.

records.claim: The completion handler checks that the payload matches the instruction's ROB tag while valid is 0 before updating to prevent overwriting newer in-flight register allocations.
records.quote: To keep track of which logical registers hold a valid digest at prediction time, RUNLTS adopts a method similar to Tomasulo's algorithm. We use a dedicated table that contains one entry per logical register. Each entry consists of a valid bit and a payload that can hold either a 14-bit tag or a 12-bit digest. At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit.
records.why: Adopting Tomasulo's algorithm requires verifying the ROB tag stored during decode matches the completing instruction before committing the payload.

records.claim: Checking inst.writes_register relies on host pipeline instruction decode metadata rather than an unproduced internal branch predictor state.
records.quote: At decode, an instruction that writes a register stores its ROB index as a tag in the corresponding entry and clears the valid bit.
records.why: The paper defines register writing as an architectural attribute of decoded instructions supplied by the execution pipeline interface.

records.claim: Integer register digests are formed by XOR folding trailing zeros/ones count at [5:0], leading zeros/ones count shifted to [8:3], and LSB bits [5:0] shifted to [11:6].
records.quote: (1) For integer registers, the digest encodes the count of leading zeros (or ones), the count of trailing zeros (or ones), and the six least significant bits, effectively capturing characteristics of addresses and round numbers.
records.why: Figure 6(a) defines the exact 3-way XOR overlap of trailing count [5:0], leading count [8:3], and Value[5:0] at [11:6], matching the unit test computation.

records.claim: Condition code flag register digests replicate the 4 flag bits three times to fill the 12-bit digest.
records.quote: (3) For condition-code flags, we replicate the four flag bits three times to fill the 12-bit digest.
records.why: Section 4.2 and Figure 6(c) explicitly specify 3-fold replication of the 4 flag bits across the 12-bit digest.

records.claim: FP32 register digests extract sign and top exponent bits from Value[31:26] positioned at digest bits [8:3].
